GraphQL Introspection Exposure Checker

Sends one real GraphQL introspection query to an endpoint URL you choose and reports whether introspection is enabled -- exposing every query, mutation, and subscription field name, and every named type, including ones no client ever links to. This is the reconnaissance step OWASP's API Security guidance names as a reason to disable introspection in production. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test.

1. Check an endpoint

Enter an endpoint URL and click Check. This tries the request directly from your browser first.

2. Or run the CLI and paste its output

If your browser could not read a response (commonly a CORS policy that doesn't allow this page's origin), the request is not subject to that restriction from a plain Node script:

node check.mjs https://api.example.com/graphql --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you pass; nothing goes through this site.

Report

Root typeField countField names

Common questions

What is GraphQL introspection and why does leaving it enabled matter?

Introspection is a set of built-in GraphQL meta-fields (__schema, __type) that let any caller ask the API to describe its own schema -- every query, mutation, subscription, type, and field name. It is essential during development, but on a production endpoint it hands an unauthenticated caller a complete map of the API's surface, including mutations and fields no real client ever links to. OWASP's API Security guidance and GraphQL's own production-hardening documentation both name disabling introspection in production as standard practice.

Why does the browser sometimes need a CLI instead of just checking the URL I type in?

The introspection query itself needs no special browser-forbidden header -- it's an ordinary POST with a JSON body -- so this page tries it directly first. Whether that succeeds depends entirely on the target's own CORS policy: some public GraphQL APIs allow requests from any origin (they're built to be called from arbitrary frontends), and for those the check runs entirely in your browser. A target with a stricter CORS policy will block the browser from reading the response even though the request reached the server -- the browser hides the response rather than reporting an error. The CLI has no such restriction, because CORS is enforced by browsers, not by Node's fetch, so it always gets a real answer.

Is it safe to run this against an endpoint?

It sends exactly one ordinary POST request carrying a read-only introspection query -- GraphQL's introspection meta-fields cannot mutate anything. It does nothing a GraphQL client wouldn't also do by querying the endpoint directly. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test, the same rule that applies to any request tool aimed at someone else's server.

Does a clean report mean the API has no other security issues?

No. This checks exactly one thing -- whether an unauthenticated introspection query succeeds -- from one request. It is not a full security assessment, does not test authenticated behaviour, field-level authorization, query depth/complexity limits, or batching/aliasing abuse, and a sensitive-sounding field name is a hint to review by hand, not proof of a missing access control. Treat a clean report as evidence about introspection specifically.

More background: why production GraphQL APIs disable introspection, and what it actually protects against.

See this checker vs. checking introspection by hand -- why testing from the API's own GraphiQL UI understates the risk, and why the mutation surface is easy to miss on a skim.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks exactly one thing -- whether an unauthenticated introspection query succeeds -- from one request. It is not a full security assessment, does not test authenticated behaviour or field-level authorization, and a sensitive-sounding field name is a hint to review by hand, not proof of a missing access control.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use it as a system of record.

Nothing is uploaded. The browser check talks straight from your tab to the endpoint you name -- never through this site -- and the CLI's request goes straight from your machine. Pasted CLI output is parsed locally in your tab; nothing you type or paste is sent anywhere. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day -- no endpoint URLs, no headers, no schema contents, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor, honouring Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control automatically. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Also worth a pass on your API: CORS misconfiguration checker covers a different response-header evidence class -- a reflected Origin rather than an enumerable schema -- and Supabase RLS exposure checker covers a database-level access-control evidence class again: whether a table returns real rows to an unauthenticated request, not a GraphQL schema at all.

vs-checking-introspection-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to the GraphQL Introspection Exposure Checker

GraphQL Introspection Exposure Checker vs. checking by hand

Pasting the standard __schema introspection query into GraphiQL, Postman, or a curl command and reading whether it comes back populated is a real, fast way to answer the yes/no question: does this endpoint answer an unauthenticated introspection query at all. It is also the method most developers already reach for, since every GraphQL server ships a playground that runs the identical query. This page names no product or company being compared against -- "checking by hand" is a generic manual habit, not a competing tool.

CaseChecking by handThis tool
Endpoint answers a plain introspection query with a populated schemaCorrectly reads as "enabled"Correctly reads as "enabled"
Endpoint returns an explicit "introspection is disabled" errorCorrectly reads as "disabled"Correctly reads as "disabled", and names the distinction from a dead or wrong-URL endpoint
Testing from a GraphiQL UI hosted on the API's own domainSame-origin request always succeeds -- says nothing about whether a third-party page could read the same responseRuns the request from this page's own origin, so a successful browser result demonstrates the target's CORS policy actually permits a cross-origin read
Schema exposes a mutation type buried among hundreds of query fieldsEasy to skim the default Query tab and never open MutationAlways parses mutationType.fields and subscriptionType.fields specifically and escalates the finding to danger the moment any mutation field exists
Field names matching sensitive wording (admin, resetPassword, impersonateUser)Requires reading every field name in a schema that can run to thousands of linesScans every query and mutation field name against a fixed sensitive-wording list and lists every match
Repeatable in CI on every deployManual, point-in-timeCLI returns a real exit code from the same classification

The gap that matters most: which origin actually asked

A GraphQL playground served by the API itself runs its introspection query from that API's own origin, and a same-origin request is never subject to CORS -- so success there proves only that the endpoint answers introspection queries at all, not that an attacker's page on a different origin could read the response too. This tool's browser check deliberately runs from a separate origin (this page), so a successful result means the target's own CORS configuration actually permits an arbitrary third-party site to read a schema dump from a visitor's browser -- the realistic exposure path, and one that testing from the API's own tooling cannot demonstrate either way. When the target's CORS policy blocks that read, the browser check correctly reports it cannot tell and the CLI -- never subject to CORS, since that restriction is enforced by browsers, not by Node's fetch -- still gets a definitive answer.

The gap that matters second: severity, not just yes/no

"Introspection is enabled" is one finding. Whether the exposed schema includes a mutation type -- the API's entire write surface, before an attacker has to guess a single field name -- is a materially different severity, and it is the one thing a person skimming a large schema by eye is most likely to miss, because GraphiQL's docs explorer opens on the Query type by default and Mutation is a separate branch to think to click into. This tool raises the finding to danger the moment mutationType.fields is non-empty, specifically so that severity does not depend on a reader remembering to open the second tab.

When to still just look

If you already know the endpoint answers introspection and you only want to browse the schema interactively -- read a specific type's fields, follow a resolver's arguments -- GraphiQL's docs explorer is the better tool for that; it is built for exploration, not for a pass/fail exposure verdict. The gap this tool closes is the two questions above: whether the exposure is reachable from an arbitrary origin, and whether the exposed surface includes writes, both of which a same-origin skim of the schema does not answer.

Common questions

What does pasting an introspection query into GraphiQL or curl actually show you?

It answers the yes/no question directly: send the standard __schema introspection query, and a populated response means introspection is enabled. That single request genuinely settles whether the endpoint answers at all -- the same request this tool sends.

Why does testing from GraphiQL hosted on the API's own domain understate the risk?

A GraphiQL or Playground UI served by the API itself makes its introspection request from that API's own origin, which any same-origin request is always allowed to do -- it says nothing about whether an arbitrary third-party page, running in a visitor's browser on a different origin, could run the same query and read the response. That is exactly what CORS governs, and it is the realistic exposure: a malicious or compromised page anywhere on the web probing the endpoint from a stranger's browser. This tool's browser check runs from this page's own origin and reports whether the target's CORS policy actually permits that cross-origin read, then falls back to a CLI (which is never subject to CORS) when it does not -- so a clean result names which of the two questions it answered rather than leaving CORS untested.

Why is spotting the mutation surface easy to miss by eye?

A real API's introspection response can list hundreds of types and enough fields that the raw JSON runs to thousands of lines. GraphiQL's docs explorer defaults to browsing the Query type, and mutationType is a separate branch of the same tree a reader has to think to open. This tool always parses mutationType.fields and subscriptionType.fields specifically, counts them, and raises the finding as danger rather than notice the moment any mutation field is present -- because an exposed write surface is a materially worse finding than an exposed read surface, and that distinction should not depend on a reader remembering to check the second tab.

Why check field names for sensitive wording automatically instead of reading the schema yourself?

Reading every field name in a schema of even moderate size for words like admin, resetPassword, or impersonateUser is tedious and easy to shortcut once the obvious top-level fields look ordinary. This tool scans every query and mutation field name against a fixed list of sensitive-operation wording and lists the matches -- still a hint to review by hand, not proof of a missing authorization check, since GraphQL field-level auth is common and no introspection response can show it. What the automated scan changes is coverage: it checks every field name, not just the ones a skim happens to land on.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure class -- whether an unauthenticated introspection query succeeds against the one endpoint you name. A clean report describes what that request found, not a guarantee the API has no other security issues.

why-disable-graphql-introspection-in-pro.text:
Why disable GraphQL introspection in production

Introspection is a set of built-in GraphQL meta-fields — __schema and __type — that let any caller ask the API to describe itself: every query, mutation, and subscription field, every custom type, and every field on every type. GraphQL tooling depends on it (schema-aware editors, codegen, GraphiQL/GraphQL Playground), which is exactly why it defaults to on in most server libraries and frameworks — a default nobody has to opt into and few people remember to turn off before shipping.

What it actually hands an attacker

Without introspection, an attacker probing an unfamiliar GraphQL endpoint has to guess field names one at a time, or find them leaked in a bundled client's source. With introspection enabled, they get the entire schema in one request: every mutation (the API's write surface), every type's fields, and every name a developer chose — including internal or debugging-only fields nobody meant to expose, and fields that hint at what a query or mutation does before the attacker has tried it once. This is reconnaissance, not exploitation by itself, but it collapses the first stage of an attack from guesswork to a single request.

Why it's standard practice to turn off, not just a hardening nice-to-have

SourceWhat it says
OWASP API SecurityNames schema introspection in production as a discoverable-surface risk to close
Apollo Server docsDisables introspection by default outside NODE_ENV=development in current versions, after years of the opposite default
graphql-yoga / express-graphqlDocument an explicit flag or plugin to disable introspection in production

Check your own endpoint

The checker on this site sends one real introspection query and reports whether it succeeded, and if so, exactly what it revealed — query, mutation, and subscription field counts, and any field names matching common sensitive-operation wording. It runs directly in your browser when the target's own CORS policy allows it, and ships a zero-dependency CLI for when it doesn't (CORS is a browser-only restriction the CLI is never subject to).

This is evidence from one request, not a full security assessment — see the checker and its disclaimer for what it does and doesn't cover. A sensitive-sounding field name is a hint to review by hand, not proof of a missing authorization check.
